The core idea behind FtTPO is to first learn a fat policy, which is dense and aims to capture the general action distribution from the offline dataset, and then to extract a sparse policy from this fat policy. The authors instantiate this framework using a two-stage policy parameterization with the general $q$-Gaussian family, which includes both heavy-tailed and sparse distributions. The fat policy is trained using a standard actor-critic approach, while the thin policy is trained using a KL divergence minimization objective, aiming to learn from the actions generated by the fat policy. The paper motivates the approach by highlighting the out-of-support action issue, where sparse policies trained directly on offline data can generate actions that are not present in the dataset, leading to poor performance. The authors argue that the two-stage approach helps mitigate this issue by first learning a dense policy and then extracting a sparse one. Empirically, the paper evaluates FtTPO on a safety-critical treatment simulation task and the standard D4RL MuJoCo benchmark.
